judgments.title: LEE KUAH SHYAN v Lee Kuah Woon & ors
judgments.catchwords: Originating Summons for declaratory relief as to the true construction of the Last Will and Testament - testator’s intention as expressed in the words of the will read as a whole, and not his unexpressed subjective wishes - Second, the court will, so far as the language permits, prefer a construction that gives every clause some operative effect over one that renders any clause meaningless - where two constructions are reasonably open, and one produces an intestacy, be it whole or partial, while the other avoids it, the court prefers the construction that avoids intestacy - the court is not entitled to make a fresh will for the testator merely because it suspects that he did not mean what he plainly said - the court may inform itself of the testator’s actual circumstances at the time he made the will, this includes his family, his property, and his business relationships, to understand what he meant by the words he used, before concluding that those words are ambiguous or deciding how any ambiguity is to be resolved. - company is a legal person distinct from its members, and that a shareholder, even one holding practically the whole of the issued capital, has no legal or equitable proprietary interest in the company’s assets.

INSURANCE: Insurance premiums — Group hospitalisation and surgical insurance policies — Recovery of alleged outstanding premiums — Payment by policyholder to insurance broker pursuant to established course of dealing — Whether payment to broker discharged policyholder's contractual payment obligations — Whether insurer's non-receipt of premiums established policyholder's indebtedness — Whether insurer proved outstanding premiums and claims excess. judgments.title: KHAIRUL IZZUDDIN BIN A RODZI v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: DRUGS: Possession of dangerous drugs – Methamphetamine – Conviction under s. 12(2) of Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 – Disputed recovery of drugs – Whether drugs recovered from appellant's trouser pocket or car porch floor – Whether prosecution established custody, control and knowledge – Whether contradictions in prosecution evidence and defence version raised reasonable doubt – Whether prosecution proved possession beyond reasonable doubt – Whether conviction safe – Dangerous Drugs Act 1952, ss. 12(2), 37(d), 39A(1). CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Appeal against conviction and sentence – Findings of fact – Appellate intervention – Failure of trial court to consider material evidence – Failure to evaluate defence witnesses and documentary evidence – Misdirection by non-direction – Whether appellate court entitled to interfere with trial court's findings of fact and credibility – Whether cumulative misdirections rendered conviction unsafe – Whether defence raised reasonable doubt – Criminal Procedure Code, ss. 173(m), 182A. CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Defence – Evaluation of defence – Bare denial and afterthought – Positive defence put to prosecution witnesses during cross-examination – Whether defence properly characterised as bare denial or afterthought – Whether trial court erred in disregarding corroborative evidence of defence witnesses – Whether failure to provide particulars of suspected third party justified rejection of defence – Whether Alcontara principle applicable where defence concerned place of recovery rather than ownership of drugs – Whether defence required to be believed to raise reasonable doubt. EVIDENCE: Credibility of witnesses – Assessment of evidence – Conflicting prosecution and defence versions – Material admissions by prosecution witnesses – Failure to consider corroborative defence evidence – Interested witnesses – Whether evidence of interested witnesses could be rejected without proper evaluation – Demeanour of accused – Reliance on unrecorded observations of hesitation and body language – Whether demeanour sufficient basis for rejecting accused's credibility – Whether contradictions relied upon by trial court material – Criminal Procedure Code, s. 271. EVIDENCE: Expert evidence – Chemist's report – Identification and weight of dangerous drugs – Laboratory analysis conducted with assistance of machine operators – Whether chemist personally involved in analysis and interpretation of results – Whether expert opinion reliable notwithstanding operation of instruments by assistants – Whether failure to call laboratory operators affected admissibility or weight of chemist's evidence – Whether adverse inference arose from failure to call operators. EVIDENCE: Adverse inference – Failure to produce documentary evidence – Sketches prepared during cross-examination – Whether failure by prosecution to tender sketches warranted adverse inference – Whether evidence withheld by prosecution – Whether sketches equally available to defence – Whether missing evidence created material gap in prosecution's case – Evidence Act 1950, s. 114(g).
judgments.judge: YA Tuan Atan Mustaffa Yussof Ahmad

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v Julasiri Bin Akilmara
judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case
